lessons.title: Absolute vs Relative Valuation: Two Different Questions

children.text: Ask ten investors whether a stock is "expensive" and you will hear two completely different kinds of answer. One says, "At ₹960 it trades at 40 times earnings, but its peers trade at 50, so it is cheap." Another says, "Its future cash flows are only worth about ₹780 a share, so at ₹960 it is expensive." Both can be doing their homework properly. They are simply answering different questions.

body.text: Absolute valuation asks what a business is worth on its own cash flows. Relative valuation asks how the market is pricing similar businesses. A stock can be cheap on one and expensive on the other at the same time.

children.text: Question 1: What Is This Business Worth on Its Own?
Absolute valuation

starts and ends with the business in front of you. You forecast the cash it will generate, choose a required return that reflects its risk, and discount that cash back to today, exactly as you did with Tarangini Cold Chain in the last lesson. The main tools:

markDefs.definition: Valuing a business from its own expected cash flows, growth and risk, without reference to what the market pays for other companies. The DCF is the main example.

children.text: Discounted cash flow (DCF).
Values the free cash flow the business generates for all its investors or for shareholders. The workhorse of this course, built step by step in Chapters 2 and 3.
Dividend discount model.
Values only the dividends shareholders receive. Useful for mature, high-payout companies such as Coal India or ITC, and a starting point for banks.
Residual income model.
Values the profit a company earns above the return shareholders demand on its book value. Especially useful for banks and NBFCs, covered in Chapter 5.

The strength of absolute valuation is independence. If the entire market is euphoric, a DCF does not care. Its weakness is that every input is a forecast, and small changes in those forecasts move the answer a lot.
Question 2: How Is the Market Pricing Similar Businesses?
Relative valuation
skips the forecast. You take a
valuation multiple
that the market is already paying for comparable companies and apply it to your company's numbers.

markDefs.definition: Valuing a business by comparing its price to a financial metric, such as earnings or book value, and benchmarking that ratio against similar companies or its own history.
A ratio of price, or enterprise value, to a financial metric. Examples are P/E (price to earnings), EV/EBITDA and P/B (price to book value).

body.caption: For example: peer median P/E × company EPS
The multiples you will use most often in Indian markets

cells: P/E
Share price to earnings per share
FMCG, IT services, pharma, consumer businesses with steady profits
EV/EBITDA
Enterprise value to operating profit before depreciation
Cement, telecom, power, metals, where debt levels differ widely
P/B
Share price to book value per share
Banks, NBFCs and insurers, where the balance sheet is the business
EV/Sales
Enterprise value to revenue
Loss-making or early-stage companies, such as new-age tech listings
Dividend yield
Dividend per share to share price
PSUs and high-payout companies bought for income

children.text: The strength of relative valuation is that it is fast and grounded in real prices. Anyone can open screener.in, pull up a peer group and see what the market pays. Its weakness is the mirror image of the DCF's strength: if the whole peer group is overpriced, relative valuation will happily tell you an overpriced stock is cheap.

columns.label: Absolute valuation
points: Question: what is this business worth on its own cash flows?
Anchor: your forecasts and required return
Output: a value per share, as a range

columns.label: Relative valuation
points: Question: is it cheap or expensive versus similar stocks?
Anchor: what the market pays for peers
Output: a premium or discount to peers or history
Strength: grounded in real, observable prices
Weakness: inherits any mispricing in the peer group
Speed: fast, needs a good peer set

children.text: Worked Example: Cheap Against Peers, Expensive Against Cash Flows

Vasudha Speciality Chemicals Ltd is a fictional NSE-listed maker of agrochemical intermediates. It trades at ₹960 and earned ₹24 per share over the last four quarters, so its P/E is 40. Four listed peers in the same niche trade at P/Es of 58, 52, 48, 44.

body.title: Trailing P/E: Vasudha vs its peer group (illustrative)

children.text: Answering Question 2: relative valuation

The peer median P/E is 50, the average of the two middle values, 52 and 48. Applied to Vasudha's EPS of ₹24, that implies a price of ₹1,200. At ₹960, Vasudha trades at a 20% discount to its peers on P/E. On this question, it looks cheap.
Answering Question 1: absolute valuation

Now build a DCF. Vasudha generated free cash flow of ₹20 per share last year. Assume, generously, that it grows at 18% a year for the next ten years, then at 5% a year forever, and that you require a 12% return. The present value of those cash flows comes to about ₹780 per share. On this question, at ₹960, it looks about 23% overvalued.
Year 10 free cash flow = ₹20 × (1.18)¹⁰ = ₹104.68 per share.
Present value of the ten years of cash flows, each discounted at 12%, = ₹269.49.
Terminal value at the end of year 10 = ₹104.68 × 1.05 ÷ (0.12 - 0.05) = ₹1570.15. Discounted back ten years at 12%, that is worth ₹505.55 today.
Total = ₹269.49 + ₹505.55 = ₹775.04, or about ₹780 per share. Chapter 3 explains terminal value properly. Here, note that it supplies most of the answer.

Both answers are correct. The disagreement is information. It tells you the market is paying roughly 50 times earnings for this whole niche, while even 18% growth for a decade only justifies about 33 times. Either the market expects something better than your generous forecast, or the whole peer group is priced for perfection. Vasudha is simply the least expensive stock in an expensive room.

body.text: The most common relative valuation mistake is "cheapest in the sector, so it must be a buy". If the sector itself is overvalued, the cheapest stock can still fall sharply when multiples compress. Always ask whether the peer group's multiple is itself reasonable.

children.text: When Each Question Leads You Astray: Two Indian Lessons
Relative valuation in a bubble: real estate, 2007-08

At the peak of the 2007 bull market, listed real estate developers looked sensibly priced against each other. The problem was that the whole group was pricing in land values and sales that the 2008 global financial crisis wiped out. DLF, then India's most valuable developer, fell by more than 80% from its early-2008 high to its 2009 low. A peer comparison inside that sector could never have warned you. Only an absolute question, "what cash will these projects actually generate?", could.
Low multiples at peak earnings: steel, FY22

Now the opposite trap. When steel prices spiked in FY22, Tata Steel reported a record consolidated profit of over ₹40,000 crore and traded at a P/E in the low single digits. On a relative basis, against the Nifty or its own history, it looked extremely cheap. But those profits were the top of a commodity cycle. Consolidated profit fell by around 80% in FY23. A P/E on peak earnings flatters a cyclical. Chapter 5 shows how to value cyclicals on normalised earnings instead.

body.text: Notice the pattern. Relative valuation fails when the whole group is mispriced. A P/E fails when the "E" is unusually high or low. Absolute valuation fails when your forecasts are wrong. No method is safe on its own, which is why serious investors ask both questions.

children.text: So Which One Should You Use?
Both, almost always, but with one of them leading depending on the business. This is the theme of the whole course, and Chapter 5 goes sector by sector. As a first map:

body.caption: Which question should lead: a first map

cells: Predictable cash flows, long history (FMCG, IT services, regulated utilities)
Absolute (DCF)
Cash flows can be forecast with reasonable confidence
Many close listed peers with similar economics (private banks, two-wheeler makers)
Relative, checked against absolute
Peer multiples are meaningful and quick to compare
Cyclicals near a peak or trough (steel, aluminium, sugar)
Absolute, on normalised earnings
Current-year multiples mislead at cycle extremes
Banks and NBFCs
P/B alongside a residual income or dividend-based model
Free cash flow is not meaningful for a lender
Loss-making, high-growth companies
Scenario-based DCF, with EV/Sales as a cross-check
P/E does not exist when there are no earnings
An entire sector or the market looks euphoric
Absolute
Relative valuation will only confirm the euphoria

body.label: A useful habit
body.value: Run both, then explain the gap
body.context: If your DCF and the peer multiple agree, you have more confidence. If they disagree, the reason for the gap is usually the most important thing you will learn about the stock.

children.text: Check Your Understanding

body.title: Which question is being answered?
body.question: A research report on a cement company says: "At 11 times EV/EBITDA, the stock trades at a 15% discount to its five-year average and to large peers." Which question is this answering?
options: What the business is worth based on its own future cash flows
How the market is pricing it compared with similar companies and its own history
What price the stock will reach in 12 months
Whether the company's cash flows will grow
body.explanation: Comparing a multiple with peers and with the company's own history is relative valuation. It tells you the stock is cheaper than usual and cheaper than peers, not what it is worth on its own cash flows, and not whether the peer group or its historical average was itself reasonable.

body.title: Implied price from a peer multiple
body.prompt: A mid-sized pharma company has EPS of ₹45. Its closest listed peers trade at a median P/E of 30. What share price does relative valuation imply, in ₹?
body.explanation: Implied price = peer median P/E × EPS = 30 × ₹45 = ₹1,350. This only tells you what the market would pay if it valued this company like its peers. It does not tell you whether 30 times earnings is a sensible multiple in the first place.

body.title: The cheapest stock in an expensive room
body.textWithBlank: A stock can trade at a discount to its peers on P/E and still trade above its ___ value.
body.explanation: Relative cheapness is measured against other prices. Intrinsic value is measured against the business's own cash flows. Vasudha was 20% below peers yet well above its DCF value.

body.title: The fund factsheet claim
body.scenario: Meera, a Chennai-based chartered accountant, holds a mid-cap mutual fund through a SIP. The latest monthly factsheet says: "Your portfolio trades at a P/E of 38 against 45 for the benchmark index, reflecting our valuation discipline." She is reassured and considers increasing her SIP.
body.prompt: What does this statement actually tell Meera, and what does it not tell her?
body.modelAnswer:
What it tells her:
1. It is a relative valuation statement. The fund's holdings are, on average, priced below the benchmark on trailing earnings.
2. The fund manager is probably avoiding the most expensive stocks in the index.

What it does not tell her:
1. Whether 45 times earnings for the benchmark is reasonable. If mid-caps as a group are expensive, a portfolio at 38 can still be expensive in absolute terms.
2. Whether the lower P/E reflects genuine value or lower quality and slower growth. Cheaper stocks are often cheaper for a reason.
3. Whether the "E" is normal. Holdings with peak-cycle earnings can show a flattering P/E.
4. Anything about future returns or timing.

A sensible next step is to look at the fund's P/E trend over several years, the benchmark's P/E against its own long-term history, and the earnings growth of the portfolio, rather than increasing her SIP on one relative comparison.

cards.definition: Values a business from its own expected cash flows, growth and risk, independent of what the market pays for other companies.
Values a business by comparing a price multiple with similar companies or with its own history.
A ratio of price or enterprise value to a metric such as earnings, EBITDA, book value or sales.
Peer multiple multiplied by the company's own metric per share, for example peer median P/E × EPS.
The middle multiple in a peer group. Preferred over the average because one extreme peer cannot distort it.
A cyclical company looking cheap on P/E because current profits are at the top of the cycle.

points: Absolute valuation asks what a business is worth on its own cash flows. Relative valuation asks how the market prices similar businesses.
The main absolute tools are the DCF, the dividend discount model and the residual income model. The main relative tools are P/E, EV/EBITDA, P/B, EV/Sales and dividend yield.
Relative valuation is fast and grounded in real prices, but inherits any mispricing in the peer group.
Absolute valuation is independent of market mood, but every input is a forecast.
A stock can be the cheapest in its sector and still be overvalued, as in the Vasudha example.
Run both. When they disagree, explaining the gap is usually the most valuable part of the analysis.

References to DLF, Tata Steel, Coal India and ITC are historical and approximate, and are not recommendations. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
